differently. Sound waves passing through the auditory canal (Figure 6.2) enter the middle ear, a structure that had to evolve when ancient fish evolved into land animals.","Because animal tissues respond to water vibrations almost the same way that water itself does, fish have relatively simple hearing receptors that would not respond well to vibrations in the air.","The structures of the middle ear and inner ear evolved to amplify sound vibrations.","When sound waves reach the middle ear, they vibrate the tympanic membrane, or eardrum. When the stirrup vibrates the oval window, it sets into motion the fluid in the cochlea (KOCK-lee-uh), the snailshaped structure of the inner ear.","According to the frequency theory in its original form, the basilar membrane vibrates in synchrony with sound waves, causing auditory nerve axons to produce action potentials at the same frequency.","For example, a sound at 50 Hz would cause 50 action potentials per second in the auditory nerve.","The downfall of this theory in its simplest form is that the refractory period limits the maximum firing rate of any neuron to about 1000 Hz, far short of the highest frequencies we hear. Although any single receptor is limited in its firing frequency, a group of receptors can have a pattern like the one represented below.","Each sound wave produces responses in the receptors that are phase-locked to the sound wave but not to one another.","A soft tone stimulates fewer neurons for each peak of the sound wave, and louder tones stimulate progressively more of them. the basilar membrane are bound together too tightly for any part to resonate like a piano string.","As information from the auditory system passes through subcortical areas, axons cross over in the midbrain to enable each hemisphere of the forebrain to get most of its input, but not all of it, from the opposite ear.","The visual and auditory systems differ in this respect: Whereas damage to the primary visual cortex (area V1) leaves someone blind, damage to the primary auditory cortex does not produce deafness.","People with damage to the primary auditory cortex have trouble with speech and music, but they identify and localize single sounds reasonably well. The cortex is not necessary for all hearing, but for processing what the information means.","When researchers record from cells in the primary auditory cortex while playing pure tones, they find that most cells have a preferred tone.","Although some cells in the auditory cortex respond well to a single tone, most cells respond best to a complex sound, such as a dominant tone and its harmonics.","Surrounding the primary auditory cortex are the secondary auditory cortex and other areas that respond mainly to meaningful The auditory cortex is important not just for hearing but also for thinking about anything related to hearing.","Human sound localization is less accurate than visual localization but nevertheless impressive.","Most birds’ alarm calls increase gradually in loudness, making them difficult for a predator to localize.","For high-frequency sounds, with a wavelength shorter than the width of the head, the head creates a sound shadow (Figure 6.7), making the sound louder for the closer ear.","In adult humans, this mechanism produces accurate sound localization for frequencies above 2,000 to 3,000 Hz and less accurate localizations for lower frequencies. How much out of phase depends on the frequency of the sound, the size of the head, and the direction of the sound.","The reason is that sounds travel faster in water than in air, so a sound","Most can localize a sudden sound of any frequency by the times of onset.","All of these methods require learning, because as a human head grows, the distance between ears increases, and humans need to recalibrate how they localize sounds. Humans can also localize whether a sound is coming from above or below, although less accurately than left vs. right.","The pinnae have an irregular shape that filters sound frequencies differently depending on their location up or down, front or back.","An estimated 4 percent of people have amusia, commonly called “tone deafness”.","Although they are not really unable to hear differences in tones, they do not detect a change less than about the difference between C and C-sharp.","They usually cannot tell whether someone is singing off-key, and they do not detect a “wrong” note in a melody. Absolute pitch (or “perfect pitch”) is the ability to hear a note and identify it—for example, “That’s a B flat.” Genetic predisposition contributes, but early musical training is also important.","In those languages, the meaning of a sound depends on its pitch, and people learn to pay close attention to pitch.","In the traditional manner of testing for absolute pitch, a researcher plays a pure note and asks someone to name it. By that method, only about one person in ten thousand qualifies, and we are tempted to think of absolute pitch as a superpower.","Although few people are totally unable to hear, many people have enough impairment to prevent speech comprehension.","Because people with conductive deafness have a normal cochlea and auditory nerve, they readily hear their own voices, conducted through the bones of the skull directly to the cochlea, bypassing the middle ear.","Because they hear themselves clearly, they may accuse others of talking too softly. Nerve deafness, or inner-ear deafness, results from damage to the cochlea, the hair cells, or the auditory nerve.","Nerve deafness can be inherited, it can result from disease, or it can result from exposure to loud noises.","It is common in people who have lost their hearing but rare in people with lifelong deafness.","It has many causes, but in some cases it resembles phantom limb. Occasionally, people with hearing loss experience auditory hallucinations, probably because something is stimulating the otherwise inactive synapses.","They especially have trouble understanding speech in a noisy room or when someone speaks rapidly.","Part of the explanation is that the brain areas responsible for language comprehension have become less active.","This trend might be just a natural deterioration, or it might be a reaction to prolonged degradation of auditory input.","If someone delays getting hearing aids, the language cortex doesn’t get its typical input, and it becomes less responsive. As cochlear hair cells die because of the aging process or anything else, the auditory cortex receives less input than usual.","That process improves hearing most of the time, but in a noisy environment, it increases the background noise just as much as the conversation.","The hearing module links the physical features of sound to a biological system that detects and interprets them. A useful review asks how the ear and auditory pathways enable recognition of sounds, discrimination of pitch, and estimates of where a sound comes from.","Mechanical events in the outer, middle, and inner ear are transformed into activity in the auditory nerve. This makes the sound available for processing by the nervous system.","Pitch depends in part on how sound is represented along the cochlea, while localization requires information that helps distinguish the source or direction of a sound.","Understand the structures of the ear, the role of hair cells, and the auditory cortex before comparing hearing impairments or age-related changes. The closing section points back to the organization that supports these functions."],"classroomCoverage":{"status":"source_structured_full_book","level":"comprehensive_book_derived","topicHeadings":10,"bullets":36,"newWords":1508,"allTopicsWithExplanations":true,"sourceScope":"verified_pdf_topic_facts_crosschecked_with_uploaded_markdown"},"classroomFigures":[{"id":"figure-6-2","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h03","number":"6.2","title":"Structures of the ear","printedPage":190,"pdfPage":208,"alt":"Excerpt from Figure 6.2 of Kalat Biological Psychology, showing structures of the ear.","image":"data:image/webp;base64,","width":1018,"height":1234,"source":"Cropped figure from user-supplied textbook PDF","cropPdfPoints":[68,62,577,679],"status":"figure number and printed page checked in PDF; crop visually reviewed by montage"}]},{"id":"bp14-m6-2","chapterId":"bp14-ch06","moduleId":"bp14-m6-2","moduleNumber":"6.2","title":"The Mechanical Senses","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":198,"printedEnd":210,"pdfStart":216,"pdfEnd":228,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"The mechanical senses include the vestibular sense, body sensation, pain, and itch. Different receptors and central pathways convey information about balance, touch, and bodily conditions."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Pain is not a simple measure of physical damage; neural and emotional factors influence it. Track where signals enter the spinal cord, how they are interpreted, and the different approaches discussed for relieving pain."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-2-study-1","text":"Balance, movement, and body position"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mechanical senses respond to movement, pressure, stretch, and other forms of physical stimulation. The vestibular system in the inner ear helps detect head movement and orientation, supporting balance and coordination with vision. Proprioceptive and somatosensory pathways convey information about the body and the contact it makes with its environment. Different receptors and neural routes specialize for different kinds of stimulation rather than sending a single generic message called 'touch'."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-2-study-2","text":"How somatosensation reaches the brain"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Receptors in skin, muscles, joints, and other tissues initiate neural signals that travel through spinal and brain pathways. The central nervous system organizes these signals into representations of body regions and sensory qualities. Touch, temperature, position, itch, and pain are related but not interchangeable experiences. Their pathways can partly differ, so a change in one sensation does not necessarily mean every aspect of feeling is lost."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-2-study-3","text":"Pain: a warning system, not a simple gauge"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Nociceptive activity provides information about potentially harmful events, but experienced pain is shaped by neural processing and circumstances. The amount of tissue damage does not map perfectly onto reported pain. Spinal circuits, descending brain influences, attention, and emotion can amplify or reduce the response. Emotional distress can be painful without a new physical injury. This distinction helps explain why pain management may target more than one biological or psychological process."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-2-study-4","text":"Relief, itch, and practical contrasts"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Pain can be altered through several methods, including medications and processes that recruit the body's own pain-modulating systems. Different approaches have limitations and cannot all be expected to work for every condition. Itch is a distinct, often irritating sensation that can promote scratching and must not simply be treated as a mild form of pain. A strong revision answer differentiates the trigger, receptor, central pathway, and subjective experience for each mechanical sense."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-2-h01","text":"Vestibular ago.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":200,"sourcePdfPage":218},{"type":"bullet","text":"It is for the same reason that you cannot surprise yourself.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":201,"sourcePdfPage":219},{"type":"bullet","text":"Your expectation of the stimulus weakens your response to it.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":201,"sourcePdfPage":219},{"type":"bullet","text":"Information from skin sensations also goes to the anterior cingulate cortex and insular cortex, which respond to the pleasantness or unpleasantness of the sensation.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":201,"sourcePdfPage":219},{"type":"bullet","text":"Two parallel strips along the nearby points on the hand, you will have an illusory experience of a single touch midway between those two points.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":201,"sourcePdfPage":219},{"type":"bullet","text":"When that happens, the activity in the primary somatosensory cortex corresponds to that and suggest that the elbow was probably around there, somewhere.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":202,"sourcePdfPage":220},{"type":"bullet","text":"One patient had an illness that axons.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":202,"sourcePdfPage":220},{"type":"bullet","text":"This phenomenon is highly variable, as some people are almost always accurate and others do no better than chance.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":202,"sourcePdfPage":220},{"type":"bullet","text":"Economic insecurity leads to depression and makes a pain feel least not of the same intensity.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":205,"sourcePdfPage":223},{"type":"bullet","text":"Presumably, the evolutionary function is that continued intense pain reason, morphine is ineffective against the sharp pain of a surgeon’s knife.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":205,"sourcePdfPage":223},{"type":"bullet","text":"Prolonged use of morphine can alter the immune system, sometimes causing a extended increase in pain.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":206,"sourcePdfPage":224},{"type":"bullet","text":"Other Ways to others.","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":206,"sourcePdfPage":224},{"type":"bullet","text":"According to gate theory, spinal cord neurons that receive messages from pain receptors also .","printedPage":206,"pdfPage":224,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":79},{"text":"The input from gentle touch or top-down influences from the .","printedPage":207,"pdfPage":225,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":83},{"text":"Unfortunately, the results so far have been disappointing, because The three semicircular canals, oriented in perpendicular planes, are filled with a fluid and lined with hair cells.","Acceleration of the head at any angle causes the fluid in one of these canals to move, just as the water in a bucket will splash if you jerk the bucket from side to side.","The fluid then pushes against the hair cells in the semicircular canals, setting up action potentials.","Unlike the saccule and utricle, the semicircular canals record only the rate of acceleration, not the position of the head at rest. Whales are 10 million times as massive as mice, but their vestibular organ is only 5 times as large.","Somatosensation is not a single sensory experience. It includes information about contact with the skin, pressure, temperature, pain, and the position and movement of the body and its joints.","Different receptors respond to different kinds of stimulation. The nervous system brings these signals together to guide posture, movement, and awareness of the body.","Touch, deep pressure, joint position, pain, and temperature rely on partly distinct receptors and pathways. A change in one channel need not affect every other form of body sensation.","Skin receptors vary in the kind and duration of pressure they detect. The Pacinian corpuscle is especially sensitive to sudden displacement and vibration rather than steady touch.","Signals from receptors in joints and muscles help the brain determine body position and movement even without visual input.","The onion-like outer structure provides mechanical support that resists gradual or constant pressure, insulating the neuron against most touch stimuli.","Only a sudden or vibrating stimulus bends the membrane, enabling sodium ions to enter and start an action potential.","On average, women can detect grooves about 1.4 mm apart, whereas men need the grooves to be about 1.6 mm apart.","The systems for cooling and heating display an interesting asymmetry: Cold-sensitive neurons in the spinal cord exhibit little response to a constant low temperature, but they respond to a drop in temperature. A cell that responds to a drop from 39° C to 33° C would also respond to a drop from 33° C to 27° C.","In contrast, heat-sensitive neurons in the spinal cord respond to the absolute temperature, and they do not adapt.","Capsaicin, found in jalapeños and other hot peppers, stimulates the receptors for painful heat. Szechuan peppers also stimulate the heat receptors, and in addition stimulate receptors that give a tingling sensation.","The body has receptors for temperature, a critical variable because overheating or overcooling the body can be","The sensation of tickle is interesting but poorly understood.","Chimpanzees respond to similar sensations with bursts of panting that resemble laughter.","Most people love humor, but most people don’t like being tickled, at least not for long.","Laughing at a joke makes you more likely to laugh at the next joke, but laughing after being tickled doesn’t change your likelihood of laughing at a joke. Actually, some people can tickle themselves—a little—if they tickle the right side of the body with the left hand or the left side with the right hand.","You might also be able to tickle yourself as soon as you wake up, before your brain is fully aroused.","Information from touch receptors in the head enters the central nervous system through the cranial nerves.","Each spinal nerve innervates (connects to) a limited area of the body called a dermatome (Figure 6.14).","For example, the third thoracic nerve (T3) innervates a strip of skin just above the nipples as well as the underarm area.","Various types of somatosensory information—such as touch, pressure, and pain—travel through the spinal cord in separate pathways toward the thalamus, which then sends impulses to different areas of the primary somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe. Two other parallel strips respond mostly to deep pressure and movement of the joints and muscles.","He still felt temperature, pain, and itch, because they depend on the unmyelinated axons.","However, he had no conscious perception of touch, which depends on myelinated axons. Recordings from his brain indicated no arousal of his primary somatosensory cortex but increased activity in the insular cortex, which responds to the emotional events and many aspects of self-awareness.","When the primary sensory cortex (S1) is inactive, either because of damage or because of temporary suppression, some people correctly “guess” the location of a touch while insisting that they did not consciously feel it.","Some languages use the same word to mean either “sick” or “depressed.” Depression is more common in women than in men, and women tend to experience more pain than men.","Much of the biological research on pain has relied on just males— sometimes humans, sometimes rodents.","The reasoning was that females were assumed to be more variable, because of their hormonal cycles.","The problem is, males and females do not react the same way to pain. Activating certain neurons in the midbrain decreases pain sensitivity in male mice, but not in females.","Researchers are beginning to pay more attention to male-female differences in pain, but that research emphasis is overdue.","Because the axons carrying pain information are thin with little or no myelin,","The thicker and faster axons convey sharp pain, whereas the thinner ones convey duller pain, such as postsurgical pain.","Mild pain releases the neurotransmitter glutamate, whereas stronger pain releases both glutamate and neuropeptides, including substance P and CGRP (ca l citonin gene-related peptide). In the spinal cord, one path conveys pain and temperature sensations, and a second path conveys touch.","The two paths differ in a way that Figure 6.15 illustrates: The pain/ temperature pathway crosses immediately from receptors to a tract on the contralateral side of the spinal cord.","Touch information travels up the ipsilateral side of the spinal cord to the medulla, and then crosses to the contralateral side.","Consider what happens to pain and touch if someone receives a cut that goes halfway through the spinal cord. Input from the pain/temperature pathway to the thalamus and then to the somatosensory cortex reports the intensity and location of the pain.","Imagine yourself in this experiment: You sit in front of a computer screen, playing a virtual ball-tossing game with two people your own age.","Experimenters monitored people’s brain activity during this virtual ball-throwing task and found increased activity in the cingulate cortex, an area responsive to the emotional aspects of pain.","Later studies found that this type of social exclusion does not always activate pain areas, but it often activates areas associated with evaluating others’ actions—that is, “why are they acting this way?”.","A study with more intense hurt feelings, based on remembering a recent romantic breakup, while looking at a photo of the ex-boyfriend or girlfriend, activated not only the cingulate cortex but also the sensory areas responsive to physical pain.","Researchers repeated the virtual ball-tossing study, but they gave some people acetaminophen and others a placebo.","Those taking acetaminophen exhibited less response in the cingulate cortex and other emotionally responsive areas. The researchers also asked college students to keep daily records about hurt feelings and social pain, while some took daily acetaminophen pills and others took a placebo.","However, there is a price to pay: People taking acetaminophen also","The brain puts the brakes on prolonged pain by opioid mechanisms — sys t ems that respond to opiate drugs and similar chemicals.","The discovery of opiate receptors was important because it revealed that opiates act on the nervous system rather than the injured tissue.","The brain produces several types of endorphins, which relieve different types of pain, such as the pain from a cut versus the pain from a burn.","However, morphine does block messages from thinner axons that convey slow, dull pain such as postsurgical pain. Anything that causes pain increases the breathing rate, and the opiates that decrease pain also decrease breathing, with potentially fatal consequences.","The input from gentle touch or top-down influences from the prefrontal cortex inhibits the pain messages in the spinal cord.","Despite much public enthusiasm for the pain-relieving potential of cannabinoids, high-quality research on this topic so far has been sparse.","Neuropathic pain is difficult to treat, and therefore any benefit from cannabinoids is encouraging. Wearing a skin patch with a high concentration of capsaicin for an hour produces a temporary burning sensation, but it causes an excessive buildup of calcium in the heat and pain neurons, and it damages those neurons’ mitochondria, rendering the cells nonfunctional until they regenerate over the next three to five months.","Unfortunately, the results so far have been disappointing, because the drugs they developed do not cross the blood-brain barrier.","Or something else altogether?” The answer is that itch is a separate sensation.","Researchers identified special receptors for itch and a special peptide that itch releases in the nervous system.","If an insect crawls slowly across your skin, that is one cause of itch.","The two types of itch sensation travel in parallel paths to the brain. Itch receptors respond slowly, and when they do, their axons transmit impulses at only half a meter per second.","Itch is useful because it directs you to scratch the itchy area and remove whatever is irritating your skin.","Your brain is not satisfied until you scratch hard enough to produce mild pain, because pain inhibits itch. The inhibitory relationship between pain and itch is clear evidence that itch is not a type of pain.","Further evidence is the demonstration that blocking itch fibers does not reduce pain.","You have learned that pain messages go to both the brain’s touch area (somatosensory cortex) and its emotion area (amygdala and related structures).","The body senses provide us with information, and they are also an important source of pleasure or displeasure.","When a dentist gives you Novocain before drilling a tooth, part of your face becomes numb.","But when you try to scratch it, you feel nothing because the touch and pain sensations are still numb. Evidently, the effects of Novocain wear off faster for itch than for touch and pain.","They’re also presented in alphabetical order with definitions in the book’s Subject Index/Glossary at the end of this book.","Different receptor properties support different tasks, such as detecting texture, adjusting a grip, or responding to a harmful stimulus."],"classroomResearch":{"title":"Evidence in context: Emotional Pain","body":"Imagine yourself in this experiment: You sit in front of a computer screen, playing a virtual ball-tossing game with two people your own age.","printedPages":[203],"pdfPages":[221],"kind":"textbook_selected_research","evidenceMethod":"single_verified_textbook_passage"},"classroomCoverage":{"status":"source_structured_full_book","level":"comprehensive_book_derived","topicHeadings":11,"bullets":47,"newWords":1750,"allTopicsWithExplanations":true,"sourceScope":"verified_pdf_topic_facts_crosschecked_with_uploaded_markdown"},"classroomFigures":[{"id":"figure-6-10","headingId":"bp14-m6-2-h01","number":"6.10","title":"Structures for vestibular sensation","printedPage":199,"pdfPage":217,"alt":"Excerpt from Figure 6.10 of Kalat Biological Psychology, showing structures for vestibular sensation.","image":"data:image/webp;base64,","width":494,"height":870,"source":"Cropped figure from user-supplied textbook PDF","cropPdfPoints":[67,63,314,498],"status":"figure number and printed page checked in PDF; crop visually reviewed by montage"}]},{"id":"bp14-m6-3","chapterId":"bp14-ch06","moduleId":"bp14-m6-3","moduleNumber":"6.3","title":"The Chemical Senses","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":211,"printedEnd":224,"pdfStart":229,"pdfEnd":242,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Taste and smell detect chemical substances through receptors and neural coding. Taste sensitivity differs among individuals, and olfaction identifies many odors through patterns of receptor activity."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The module also considers synesthesia, in which stimulation in one sense is associated with an experience in another. Compare the coding strategies used by taste and olfaction instead of treating all chemical senses alike."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-3-study-1","text":"Taste as chemical detection"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Taste begins when dissolved substances interact with receptor cells in taste buds. The system contributes to decisions about food and potentially harmful substances. Different receptor mechanisms respond to broad taste qualities, such as sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. The same taste quality can involve more than one molecular mechanism, and the perceived flavor of food includes smell and other sensations. A food experience cannot be explained by tongue receptors alone."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-3-study-2","text":"Coding and individual variation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Taste information moves through cranial nerves and central pathways, and neural activity represents both stimulus quality and intensity. People can differ substantially in sensitivity to particular bitter compounds or other taste stimuli because of biological variation and experience. Preferences are also affected by learning and bodily state. A sensitivity difference is not the same thing as a difference in preference: someone may detect a taste accurately yet dislike it."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-3-study-3","text":"Olfaction and its special route"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Odor molecules bind to receptors in olfactory tissue, activating populations of neurons whose combined activity distinguishes many odorants. Signals travel to the olfactory bulb and onward to areas involved in perception, memory, and emotion. The olfactory system is organized differently from a simple one-receptor-for-one-smell model. It is especially easy to notice the integration of senses when a blocked nose changes the flavor of food."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-3-study-4","text":"Synesthesia and integrated perception"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Synesthesia refers to experiences in which stimulation in one domain reliably evokes an additional experience in another, such as particular colors associated with letters. It illustrates how perceptual systems can interact and how people's subjective worlds vary. It should not be confused with the normal contribution of smell to flavor. Across this module, distinguish the chemicals that initiate a signal from the neural codes and experiences that result."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h01","text":"Taste"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Vision, hearing, and touch provide useful information for many purposes, but taste is useful only for telling us whether to swallow something or spit it out.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That function is more important for some species than for others.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because they eat only fish, and swallow them whole, they have little need for the sense of taste.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Taste results from stimulation of the taste buds , the receptors on the tongue.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When we talk about the taste of food, we generally mean flavor, which combines taste and smell.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Taste and smell axons converge onto many of the same cortical cells, enabling them to combine their influences .","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h02","text":"Taste Receptors"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The receptors for taste are not true neurons but modified skin cells.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Like neurons, taste receptors have excitable membranes and release neurotransmitters to excite neighboring neurons, which in turn transmit information to the brain.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Like skin cells, however, taste receptors are gradually sloughed off and replaced, each one lasting 10 to 14 days .","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mammalian taste receptors are in taste buds located in papillae on the surface of the tongue (Figure 6.19).","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A given papilla may contain up to 10 or more taste buds , and each taste bud contains about 50 receptor cells.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In adult humans, taste buds lie mainly along the edge of the tongue.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Then try it again on the edge of your tongue and notice the taste.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It will seem as if you are moving the taste to the center of your tongue.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"You attribute the taste you had on the side of your tongue to any other spot you stroke .","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h03","text":"How Many Kinds of Taste Receptors?"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditionally, people in Western society have described tastes in terms of sweet, sour, salty, and bitter.","sourcePrintedPage":211,"sourcePdfPage":229,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One way to identify taste receptor types is to find procedures that alter one receptor but not others.","sourcePrintedPage":212,"sourcePdfPage":230,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, chewing a miracle berry (native to West Africa) gives little taste itself but temporarily changes sweet receptors.","sourcePrintedPage":212,"sourcePdfPage":230,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Miracle berries contain a protein—miraculin—that modifies sweet receptors, enabling acids to stimulate them .","sourcePrintedPage":212,"sourcePdfPage":230,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"(available via the Internet), anything acidic will taste sweet in addition to its usual sour taste for the next half hour.","sourcePrintedPage":212,"sourcePdfPage":230,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most toothpastes contain sodium lauryl sulfate, a chemical that intensifies bitter tastes while it coats the sweet receptors and prevents anything from reaching them .","sourcePrintedPage":213,"sourcePdfPage":231,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This demonstration is probably risky for anyone with diabetes, because G. sylvestre also alters sugar absorption in the intestines.","sourcePrintedPage":213,"sourcePdfPage":231,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The overall point of these demonstrations is that we do have receptors that are sensitive to one taste or another.","sourcePrintedPage":213,"sourcePdfPage":231,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This phenomenon, called adaptation , reflects the fatigue of receptors sensitive to sour tastes.","sourcePrintedPage":213,"sourcePdfPage":231,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although we have long known that people have at least four kinds of taste receptors, several types of evidence suggest a fifth, glutamate, as in monosodium glutamate (MSG).","sourcePrintedPage":213,"sourcePdfPage":231,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Water replaces the bicarbonate ions usually present in the saliva on the tongue, and when it does so it changes the acid-to-base ratio and mildly stimulates the same receptors that detect sour tastes.","sourcePrintedPage":213,"sourcePdfPage":231,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers stimulated rats’ brain cells responsive to taste with an electrical pattern matching that for quinine.","sourcePrintedPage":213,"sourcePdfPage":231,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h04","text":"Mechanisms of Taste Receptors"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Recall that a neuron produces an action potential when sodium ions cross its membrane.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A saltiness receptor simply permits sodium ions on the tongue to cross its membrane, and thereby detects the presence of sodium .","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After a molecule binds to one of these receptors, it activates a G protein that releases a second messenger within the cell.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People have two types of sweetness receptors and two types of umami receptors, each with somewhat different sensitivities .","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Bitter taste used to be a puzzle because bitter substances include a long list of dissimilar chemicals.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The answer is that we have not one bitter receptor but a family of approximately 30 that respond to different sets of compounds .","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Our large number of bitter receptors enable us to detect a great variety of dangerous chemicals.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Bitter chemicals are toxic, and the body does what it can to expel them.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h05","text":"Taste Coding"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Let’s contrast two ways of coding sensory information.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Anything that excites a pain axon reaches the brain as a pain sensation.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In contrast, color vision requires an across-fiber pattern, or","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The only way to resolve the ambiguity is to compare it with the responses of the other types of cones.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most taste receptors respond only to one type of chemical, but some respond to both sweet and salty, or sweet and umami.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The receptors feed into neurons that might respond just to one taste, or to several .","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"By the time information reaches cells in the insula in the cortex (Figure 6.21), most cells respond most strongly to one taste, partly to others also, and in many cases also to odors, hunger, emotions, and other influences.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The insula is not arranged in clusters of cells that respond mainly to one taste or another .","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the response of any cortical taste cell is ambiguous, the meaning requires a comparison across cells .","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h06","text":"Variations in Taste Sensitivity"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"And if we ask people to describe how strong various foods taste, they agree on which foods have bland, strong, or very strong flavors.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, when you say some food has a strong taste, you mean that it is strong compared to your other experiences.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Some people have three times as many taste buds as other people do on the fungiform papillae near the tip of the tongue (Figure 6.22).","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Those with the greatest number are called supertasters , and those with average or below-average numbers are tasters or non-tasters (a misleading term).","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Several genes have significant effects , but the variation also depends on age, hormones, and other influences.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That tendency is probably adaptive, because a pregnant person needs to be careful to avoid harmful foods.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with the most taste buds tend to dislike strongly flavored foods, especially foods with a bitter taste.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, these tendencies have many exceptions, because food preferences depend on familiarity and other influences.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, non-tasters are common in India, where the food is spicy, and also in Britain, with relatively bland foods.","sourcePrintedPage":214,"sourcePdfPage":232,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The smell of a sweaty female increases a male’s testosterone secretions, especially if the female is near her time of ovulation.","sourcePrintedPage":216,"sourcePdfPage":234,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h07","text":"Olfaction"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Olfaction, the sense of smell, is the response to chemicals that contact the membranes inside the nose. Olfaction contributes to selecting and enjoying food. Its contribution to flavor is apparent when the nasal passages are blocked.","sourcePrintedPage":216,"sourcePdfPage":234,"sourceMethod":"manual_paraphrase_checked_against_pdf"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h08","text":"Olfactory Receptors"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The neurons responsible for smell are the olfactory cells that line the olfactory epithelium in the rear of the nasal air","sourcePrintedPage":217,"sourcePdfPage":235,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In mammals, receptors are on the olfactory cell’s cilia (threadlike dendrites) that extend into the mucous surface of the nasal passage.","sourcePrintedPage":217,"sourcePdfPage":235,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Humans have several hundred types of olfactory receptors, while rats and mice have about a thousand and elephants have about two thousand .","sourcePrintedPage":217,"sourcePdfPage":235,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Like metabotropic neurotransmitter receptors, each olfactory receptor protein traverses the cell membrane seven times and responds to a chemical outside the cell (an odorant molecule) by triggering changes in a G protein inside the cell.","sourcePrintedPage":217,"sourcePdfPage":235,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Olfactory receptors are vulnerable to damage because they are exposed to the air.","sourcePrintedPage":217,"sourcePdfPage":235,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Each olfactory neuron axon contains copies of its olfactory receptor protein, which it uses like an identification card to find its correct partner .","sourcePrintedPage":217,"sourcePdfPage":235,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, if the entire olfactory surface is damaged at once by a blast of toxic fumes so that the system has to replace all","sourcePrintedPage":217,"sourcePdfPage":235,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"the receptors at the same time, many of them fail to make the correct connections, and olfactory experience does not fully recover .","sourcePrintedPage":218,"sourcePdfPage":236,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h09","text":"Olfactory Coding"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The diversity of olfactory receptors makes possible narrow specialization of functions.","sourcePrintedPage":218,"sourcePdfPage":236,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Each olfactory cell has only one receptor type, and most receptors respond to either just one chemical or several closely related chemicals.","sourcePrintedPage":218,"sourcePdfPage":236,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Some receptors respond synergistically; that is, they respond to a combination of two chemicals, but hardly at all to either one alone .","sourcePrintedPage":218,"sourcePdfPage":236,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although the receptors are arranged haphazardly along the nasal cavity, all the receptors sensitive to a particular chemical or combination of chemicals connect to a single cluster in the olfactory bulb, called a glomerulus (Figures 3.12 and 6.25) .","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When we get to the primary olfactory cortex, known as the piriform cortex , things are different.","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Whereas each glomerulus responds to just one chemical, each cell in the piriform cortex responds to a combination of chemicals, such as the smell of berries or melons .","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because each neuron responds to a combination of influences, its response does not identify a single odorant.","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h10","text":"Individual Differences"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most of the genes controlling olfactory receptors have variant forms, and on average, two people chosen at random probably differ in about 30 percent of their olfactory receptor genes .","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sensitivity to mushroom odor remains nearly constant as people age, sensitivity to onion odor declines moderately, and sensitivity to rose odor declines greatly .","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A sharp decline in odor sensitivity is often an early symptom of Alzheimer’s disease or Parkinson’s disease .","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many people who were infected by the worldwide pandemic of COVID-19 suffered an impaired sense of smell, with slow recovery over weeks.","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The virus probably does not enter human neurons, but it damages the skin cells that support the olfactory receptors in the nose .","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Humane females detect odors more readily than males, at all ages and in all cultures that researchers have tested","sourcePrintedPage":219,"sourcePdfPage":237,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Males, prepubescent females, and post-menopausal females do not demonstrate hormones.","sourcePrintedPage":220,"sourcePdfPage":238,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-3-h11","text":"Synesthesia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Finally, also.","sourcePrintedPage":220,"sourcePdfPage":238,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People reporting synesthesia have increased amounts of gray matter in .","sourcePrintedPage":220,"sourcePdfPage":238,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers found 10 people with synesthesia whose associations matched or .","sourcePrintedPage":220,"sourcePdfPage":238,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Only a small percentage of children who play with these magnets develop
